newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-LYLE TURNS BACK CLOCK, SHARES LEAD AT GREENSBORO CLASSIC.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-LYLE TURNS BACK CLOCK, SHARES LEAD AT GREENSBORO CLASSIC.

text.p: Sandy Lyle used an old caddie and an old putting stance to tie for the lead on Thursday after the first round at the $1.9 million Greater Greensboro Chrysler Classic.

Lyle, who won here in 1986 and 1988 back when he was one of the world's premier golfers, birdied his first three holes in sloppy conditions on the Forest Oaks course, which played relatively easily because players were allowed preferred lies.

He reeled off seven birdies and one bogey to join Mike Hulbert and Robert Damron at six-under 66, one stroke ahead of eight players including U.S. Ryder Cup captain Tom Kite and Australian Steve Elkington, this year's leading PGA Tour money winner.
It was a major turnaround for Lyle, who shot an opening round 79 on his way to missing the cut at last week's PGA Tour event, the MCI Heritage Clasic at Hilton Head Island.
"I was feeling pretty low after last week," Lyle admitted. "I played very badly. The frustration level was going through the roof.
"My caddie (Max Cunningham) sacked me. I wasn't sure how I was going to handle this week."
Lyle, 39, looked no further for a new caddie than wife Jolande. She used to carry her husband's bag occasionally, although she hasn't done so recently.
"She's had a very good calming effect," continued Lyle, the 1985 British Open and 1988 Masters champion. "I'm very pleased. Another three rounds like that would be very nice."

Along with a change of caddie, Lyle also changed his putting set-up. On Wednesday night, while watching an old tape of his victory here 11 years ago, he noticed that he stood with his hips squarer to the target in those days.

Figuring he had nothing to lose after three-putting 10 times at the Masters a fortnight ago, Lyle squared up his stance and was delighted with the improvement as he ran in four of his birdies from eight feet or longer, and did not once three-putt.
Hulbert, meanwhile, made the day's best start with birdies at the first five holes, highlighted by a 30-footer at the first.
"That maybe turned the green light on," said the 39-year-old journeyman who has three PGA Tour victories.
Tour rookie Damron, on the other hand, made his move on the back nine, which he played in five under.
"I've been hitting the ball very well the last three or four weeks," said Damron, who has been unhappy with his putting. "On the back nine today I made most of the putts I felt I should have made."
